- Acme will be the controller for customer data; Redwood will act as a processor for inference requests and related telemetry.
- Primary concerns: DPA execution timeline, which SCC module(s) Acme requires, and a vendor security questionnaire for standard SOC 2 + GDPR evidence.

2) Which SCC module(s) does Acme require (please indicate module numbers or paste the exact text from your template) — this determines whether we need to include subprocessors/SaaS-adjacent clauses.
3) Can you start the vendor security questionnaire? If you want, we can pre-populate answers for the SOC 2 and encryption sections.

Proposed next steps:
- Naomi (legal) to review Acme comments and coordinate DPA redlines.
- Rishi (engineer) to run a short technical follow-up (30 min) to cover data residency, logging, and encryption-in-transit/at-rest.
- Emily to confirm SCC module preference and the DPA owner at Acme.

I can schedule the tech follow-up for next Tue/Wed — what works for your team?

Thanks again — looking forward to keeping momentum on this.

Hi Emily —

Quick technical note from the infra/architecture side:
- Redwood operates as a processor for customer inference traffic; controllers retain control over data classification and retention windows via API/route-level settings.
- For SCCs: we typically recommend Module 1 (Transfer of personal data to processors) and include the standard Processor Annex that lists subprocessors and data flow diagrams. In most SaaS-to-SaaS relationships Module 1 + the Processor Annex suffices. If Acme’s template explicitly requires Module 2 (onward transfers to sub-processors) we can expand the annex accordingly.
- Data residency: we can pin inference to US regions for Acme and limit backups to customer-specified regions if required (we'll need an enterprise config).

I attached the SCC mapping matrix for your legal team to review; it shows which modules we support today and the typical language we expect to include. Happy to join a quick legal call if Naomi wants to go through row-by-row.

– Rishi
